connector: At the end of Chapter 9, Harriet stood in Philadelphia, free and earning her own money. But her family was still in Maryland. She told William Still she would go down, like Moses into Egypt, to lead them out. In Chapter 10, look for what makes each trip happen, and what each trip leads to.

a.raw: harriet walked carefully south her steps were silent and her heart beat loudly
a.fixed: Harriet walked carefully south. Her steps were silent, and her heart beat loudly.
a.why: Capital H on Harriet; a period ends the first sentence; capital H starts the second; a comma before and joins two complete thoughts. Carefully and loudly are adverbs that tell how.

b.raw: mary ann sailed quietly up the bay harriet waited anxiously in baltimore
b.fixed: Mary Ann sailed quietly up the Bay. Harriet waited anxiously in Baltimore.
b.why: Capital M and A on Mary Ann (a name); capital B on the Bay, the name of a place; a period ends the first sentence; capital H on Harriet; capital B on Baltimore (a city). Quietly and anxiously are adverbs that tell how.

fill1.h1: When you say your feelings out loud, you push them out of you. Which root means push?
fill1.why: press means push: ex + press = push out.

fill2.h1: Pressing a stamp into wax leaves a mark. Which root means push?
fill2.why: press means push: im + press = push in, leave a mark.

fill3.h1: A box keeps everything together inside it. Which root means hold?
fill3.why: tain means hold: con + tain = hold together.

fill4.h1: If you keep something and won’t let it go, which root means hold?
fill4.why: tain means hold: re + tain = hold back, keep.

notes.wgrd: In history, things happen for reasons. Name the event, look back for what made it happen, and say it with because: Harriet did this because …
vocab: The act of ending something, especially slavery.
A guide on the Underground Railroad; or, the person who runs a train.
To make a thought, feeling, or idea known to others.
notes.wordParts: press means “push” and tain means “hold”: express, impress, contain, obtain.
notes.grammar: An adverb tells more about a verb: how, when, or where. Many end in -ly, like slowly. Some don’t, like again and outside.
notes.spelling: The suffixes -ive, -al, and -ic turn a word into a describing word: act → active, music → musical, hero → heroic. Look at the base word first. Sometimes a letter drops, like a silent e.

catcher.title: Because …
catcher.intro: Pick one trip in Ch. 10. Write what made it happen, and what happened because of it.

wordgame.voice: Tap a root, then the word it finishes. Or drag the root onto the word. Ask what each word is about: pushing, or holding?

why.t: In Chapter 2, Harriet’s mother, Old Rit, finishes a patchwork quilt, the family’s only treasure. Years later, in Chapter 12, Harriet tucks that same quilt over her parents’ legs as she drives them out of slavery. press means push, and tain means hold. Each right word sews one patch into the quilt. Four each lesson, until the quilt is finished.

wordgame.winDay: Four more patches are sewn in. The next lesson’s words add more.
wordgame.win: Old Rit’s quilt is finished, and a North Star is stitched across its middle. press = push, tain = hold.

transcripts.welcome: Hey, it’s Marcus. Last time, Harriet stood in Philadelphia, free, and said she would go back for her people. Chapter 10 is called Why Not Every Man? It comes from a song she sang in the fields as a girl. Today’s question: once you’re free, what do you owe the people still waiting?
transcripts.read: Chapter 10 moves fast, one trip after another. Keep a list: who Harriet brings out each time, and what goes wrong. Watch a cold river, a door that should open and doesn’t, and a man talking to himself near a swamp. Ask what made each trip happen.
transcripts.morphology: New roots this week. One means push. One means hold. Think of a printing press pushing ink onto paper, or a jar that holds jam. Every word in the quilt is pushing something or holding something. Ask which one, then sew.

virtue.title: Why isn’t it enough?
virtue.intro: In Chapter 10, Harriet is free, but she keeps going back into Maryland: for her sister Mary Ann, her brother James, and William Henry. In two years she leads forty people out. She tells William Still, “My people must go free.”
virtue.line: Write one sentence: Why isn’t Harriet’s own freedom enough for her?
virtue.name: freedom
